answer: Agents can make high-value actions contingent on a slowly accumulated, nontransferable reputation earned through repeated work that independent peers verify and that is periodically challenged with unpredictable tasks. A new identity cannot simply forge that history, while copied identities must each spend time and stake to build it. A prism of cross-checks—random audits plus agreement among unrelated reviewers—makes collusion easier to detect; the nadir is that reputation still decays when reviewers or tasks are compromised, so it raises the attack cost rather than proving unique personhood.
